"The excerpt argues that the old 19th-century “great man” theory of history remains surprisingly influential, even though later schools of thought, including egalitarian, Marxist, and “history from below” approaches, challenged it. That theory, associated here with Thomas Carlyle, holds that history is shaped above all by a small number of extraordinary individuals whose talent, force of character, courage, and charisma allow them to redirect the course of events. Carlyle is said to have placed figures such as Aristotle, Julius Caesar, Napoleon, Martin Luther, and the prophet Muhammad in this category, treating them as exceptional heroes whose impact was profound and lasting, while ordinary people were reduced to passive followers and admirers.

The article’s tone is skeptical and critical of this view, calling it “daft” even while acknowledging its enduring appeal. Its persistence seems to come from how seductive it is to imagine history as the work of singular, commanding personalities rather than broader social forces or collective movements. The passage then shifts from historical theory to the present, arguing that men who still imagine themselves in this heroic tradition often see themselves as destined leaders with a special mission, superior insight, or even a sacred duty to save nations and peoples. These figures are portrayed as arrogant and ruthless enough to force their beliefs on others.

Crucially, the excerpt says that in the modern era such supposedly “great” men are usually not genuine heroes but anti-heroes or outright villains. While they still possess considerable power, their influence is framed as dangerous rather than admirable, suggesting that the cult of heroic leadership now often masks authoritarianism, egotism, and destructive ambition rather than greatness."
